# Objects and data frames {#objects-and-data-frames .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 1
:::

::: notes
Section one starts at the very bottom, with the places where you type R and the way in which R answers. Then come the two pieces from which everything else is built: objects, which give a value a name, and vectors, which hold a run of values. One small fact about vectors carries most of the arithmetic of the course, that the mean of a run of ones and zeros is a share. We end with the data frame, the table in which R keeps a dataset, and with a first task of your own.
:::

## The console and the script {#the-console-and-the-script .smaller}

::: {.fs-130}
```r
1014 - 23
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-out-subtract
1014 - 23
```

::: {.small}
- **The console** runs a line as soon as you press Enter, and keeps no record of how a result was reached
- **A script** is a plain text file ending in `.R`. Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) sends the line under the cursor to the console, and the script keeps the line
- Try things in the console, and move anything that matters into the script
:::

::: notes
In your IDE there are two places to type R. The console runs a line the moment you press Enter. Type one thousand and fourteen minus twenty-three, and R answers nine hundred and ninety-one, the emails that reached a housing authority out of the thousand and fourteen that were sent. The one in square brackets is not part of the answer, because R numbers the values that it prints. [advance] A script keeps what you type. Put the same line in your new script, leave the cursor on it, and press Control and Enter: the line goes to the console and runs there. [advance] The rule of the course is to try things in the console and to move anything that matters into the script, because the script records how a result was reached, and the console forgets it when the session ends.
:::

## Objects and vectors {#objects-and-vectors .smaller}

::: {.fs-130}
```r
emails_sent <- 1014               # a number
first_name  <- "Santiago"         # text, called a character string, in quotes
emails_sent - 23

delivered <- c(308, 326, 357)     # white, Black and Hispanic names
replies   <- c(177, 198, 188)
replies / delivered               # one division for each group
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-out-vectors
emails_sent <- 1014
emails_sent - 23
delivered <- c(308, 326, 357)
replies   <- c(177, 198, 188)
replies / delivered
```

::: {.small}
`<-` gives a value a name, and the name then stands in for the value. `c()` combines values of one type into a **vector**, and arithmetic works on a whole vector at once.
:::

::: notes
R works by putting values into named objects. The arrow, typed as a less-than sign and a hyphen, assigns: emails sent gets one thousand and fourteen, and from then on the name stands in for the number, so emails sent minus twenty-three gives nine hundred and ninety-one again. Names are case-sensitive, and asking for a name that was never assigned gives the message "object not found", which you will meet whenever a line uses an object that an earlier line was meant to make. A vector is a run of values of one type, made with c, for combine. These two hold, for the white, the Black and the Hispanic names in turn, the emails that reached an official and the replies that came back, and one division gives the three reply rates. The six numbers were typed by hand, and the third section computes them from the file.
:::

## Means and missing values {#means-and-missing-values .smaller}

::: {.fs-130}
```r
greeted <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0)       # five replies, 1 = opened with the name of the sender
mean(greeted)                     # the share of 1s

greeted <- c(1, 0, NA, 1, 0)      # the third reply carries no greeting code
mean(greeted)
mean(greeted, na.rm = TRUE)       # the share among the four replies with a code
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-out-means
greeted <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0)
mean(greeted)
greeted <- c(1, 0, NA, 1, 0)
mean(greeted)
mean(greeted, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.fragment .small}
The file has missing values of three kinds: the `r n_bounced` emails that bounced have no reply, an email without a reply has no greeting, and `r n_uncoded` replies were never coded. The course never uses `na.rm = TRUE` without saying which rows it removes.
:::

::: notes
One small fact carries most of the arithmetic of the course. When a vector holds only ones and zeros, its mean is the share of ones, because the mean adds the values, which counts the ones, and divides the sum by the number of values. The outcome of the claim of the housing-audit case, whether a reply opened with the name of the sender, is stored in exactly this way, so the share of replies that greeted the sender by name is a mean. Real data have gaps, which R marks NA, for not available, and any calculation that meets one returns NA, because the answer cannot be known. The argument na dot rm removes the missing values first. [advance] In our file a missing value can mean three different things, and deciding what to do with each kind is part of the analysis.
:::

## Data frames {#data-frames .smaller}

::: {.fs-130}
```r
emails <- tibble::tibble(
  name  = c("Brett", "Santiago", "Emily"),
  reply = c(1, 1, 0),
  named = c(1, 0, NA)
)
emails
emails$named                      # one column, as a vector
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-out-tibble
emails <- tibble::tibble(
  name  = c("Brett", "Santiago", "Emily"),
  reply = c(1, 1, 0),
  named = c(1, 0, NA)
)
emails
emails$named
```

::: {.small}
A **data frame** is a table: vectors of equal length standing side by side as columns, with one row for each observation. A **tibble** is a data frame that prints its size and the type of each column, `<chr>` for text and `<dbl>` for numbers.
:::

::: notes
A data frame is how R stores a table: vectors of the same length standing side by side as columns, with one row for each observation, and almost everything in the course is a data frame. This one is built by hand, with three emails, the name that signed each, whether a reply came and whether the reply greeted the sender by name. The third email shows why a greeting can be missing: no reply came, so there was no greeting to code. The part before the two colons names the package from which the function comes, which the next section explains. A tibble prints its size on the first line and the type of each column under its name. The dollar sign pulls one column out as a vector, which is often the quickest way to look at a single column, and for reshaping a table the course uses the verbs of the third section.
:::

## Hands-on 1 – The reply rate {#hands-on-1-the-reply-rate .smaller}

::: {.small}
In your script, with the two vectors of the last slides:
:::

::: {.fs-130}
```r
sum(replies) / sum(______)
replies[3]
Emails_sent
```
:::

::: {.small}
1. Fill the blank so that the line divides all the replies by all the delivered emails, which gives the share of the delivered emails that drew a reply, whatever the name
2. Square brackets pick out a value by its position: the third is the replies to the Hispanic names
3. A capital E makes another name: read what R says
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The share is `r sprintf("%.6f", n_replies / n_delivered)`, the reply rate of the `r n_delivered` delivered emails, which the second section reaches again from the file.
:::

::: notes
Your turn, on your own machine, with three short lines in your script. First, fill the blank so that the line divides all the replies by all the delivered emails, which gives the share of the delivered emails that drew a reply, whatever the name that signed each email. Second, pick out the third value of the replies with square brackets, the replies to the Hispanic names. Third, type the name of the first object with a capital E and read what R says, because you will meet that message many times, and it always means that R has no object of that name in the session. Take the time you need, and if a line stops with an error that you cannot read, tell me. [advance] The share is a little under fifty-seven per cent, and we will reach it again from the file.
:::
